can you take a look at this: 

The proper fix is to change Entire's transcript-storage pipeline. Raising the timeout is only a
  temporary workaround.

  Entire should retain Codex's original rollout untouched, but create a portable checkpoint copy in
  this order:

  raw Codex rollout
      ↓
  remove encrypted reasoning/compaction payloads
      ↓
  externalize inline images
      ↓
  redact remaining readable text
      ↓
  chunk and store in Git

  Today, Entire effectively redacts first and sanitizes later—or does not sanitize at all in the
  temporary Stop path. You can see the wrong ordering in /Users/thomi/Projects/entire-cli/cmd/entire/
  cli/checkpoint/persistent.go:1040: redaction happens at line 1041, while Codex sanitization only
  happens at line 1053.

  Concretely, I would:

  1. Introduce a generic PrepareTranscriptForStorage agent capability.

     Codex's implementation would call the existing /Users/thomi/Projects/entire-cli/cmd/entire/cli/
     agent/codex/transcript.go:388, removing encrypted_content, compaction payloads, and other non-
     portable state before secret detection.

  2. Use that transformation in every checkpoint path.

     This includes Stop/ephemeral checkpoints, committed checkpoints, task checkpoints, and
     finalization. Currently Stop writes the raw transcript into metadata at /Users/thomi/Projects/
     entire-cli/cmd/entire/cli/lifecycle.go:737, after which the generic metadata walker redacts the
     whole thing.

  3. Externalize images before redaction.

     Entire already has a Codex image codec and the correct extract-before-redact ordering in /Users/
     thomi/Projects/entire-cli/cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_condensation.go:309. That pipeline
     should be centralized and reused.

  4. Make transcript checkpointing incremental.

     Store transcripts as append-only chunks and reuse the previous redacted Git blobs. On each Stop,
     Entire should sanitize and redact only records appended since the previous Stop. If the rollout
     was truncated, replaced, or the redaction configuration changed, it can fall back to a full
     rebuild.

  5. Add detailed timings and a performance regression test.

     A 25 MB existing transcript plus one new turn should checkpoint in roughly constant time—ideally
     under one or two seconds—not rescan the preceding 25 MB.

  The important distinction: merely skipping secret scanning for encrypted_content is incomplete
  because it would still preserve megabytes of useless ciphertext in every checkpoint. Entire should
  remove it from its copy while leaving Codex's original rollout intact. Chunking without incremental
  redaction is also insufficient because it would still scan the complete transcript before producing
  the chunks.
I'll dig into the actual code to check whether these claims hold up.

content.text:
I verified every claim against this checkout (their paths are from a different clone, so line numbers shifted slightly). **The diagnosis is correct and the ordering bug is real.** Here's what holds up, what doesn't, and one thing the note misses that constrains the fix.

## Verified

| Claim | Status |
|---|---|
| Redact-before-sanitize in the committed path | ✅ `checkpoint/persistent.go:1041` redacts, `:1053` sanitizes. The in-memory path is worse — it's redacted even earlier, at `strategy/manual_commit_condensation.go:319` (`redactOrDrop`), on the raw rollout. |
| Stop path never sanitizes | ✅ `lifecycle.go:744` writes the raw rollout to `.entire/sessions/<id>/full.jsonl`; the shadow-tree walker (`ephemeral.go:990` → `createRedactedBlobFromFile`) redacts every blob and never calls `SanitizePortableTranscript`. |
| Extract-before-redact already exists and is the right pattern | ✅ `manual_commit_condensation.go:314` externalizes images, `:319` redacts, with a comment explaining exactly why that order is required. |
| No incremental redaction anywhere | ✅ Every Stop redacts the full transcript from byte 0. `PrecomputeTranscriptBlobs` (`persistent.go:2091`) only shares blobs *within* one write, not across checkpoints. |

## The numbers back the argument hard

Synthetic Codex rollout, ~100KB encrypted reasoning per turn (M4 Max):

| Size | redact only | sanitize + redact | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.7 MB | 10.3 s | 17 ms + 1 ms | 574× |
| 6.8 MB | 16.6 s | 42 ms + 1 ms | 381× |
| 27.4 MB | 46.9 s | 170 ms + 5 ms | 267× |

Throughput: **0.26 MB/s vs 164 MB/s**. Sanitization removes **99.7%** of the bytes. Base64 ciphertext is the pathological input for the entropy layer (`secretPattern` + Shannon ≥ 4.5 in `redact/redact.go:23`) — every ciphertext token is a candidate. Real rollouts have more ordinary prose, so expect a smaller multiplier, but the direction and order of magnitude are right, and this is plainly the timeout cause.

## Two corrections to the framing

**"preserve megabytes of useless ciphertext in every checkpoint" — only the local shadow branch.** Pushed `entire/checkpoints/v1` transcripts *are* sanitized (`persistent.go:1053`, and again at finalize `:2062`). The ciphertext bloat is confined to the local shadow branch, and it's a fresh multi-MB blob per Stop since the rollout grows every turn. Still worth fixing, but it's local disk, not published data.

**"Add detailed timings" — mostly already there.** `perf.Start` spans wrap chunking and blob writes, and `redactOrDrop` returns a duration that gets logged. What's genuinely missing is the *regression test*; hang it off the existing `strategy/postcommit_bench_test.go` or `integration_test/hook_bench_test.go`.

## The blocker the note doesn't mention

Sanitization **deletes whole lines** (`codex/transcript.go:405-435`: `compaction` / `compaction_summary` → dropped), but `CheckpointTranscriptStart` is counted on the **raw** rollout (`countTranscriptItems` at `manual_commit_condensation.go:1088`) and then used to slice the **stored, sanitized** transcript (`explain.go:1977`, whose own comment says "CheckpointTranscriptStart indexes the stored format"). That offset also feeds the compact boundary: `writeCompactTranscript` passes the raw-coordinate `startLine` over post-sanitize bytes (`persistent.go:1153-1157`).

So a Codex session with compaction events already has drifting offsets today — and moving sanitization earlier changes that drift rather than removing it. **Any `PrepareTranscriptForStorage` capability has to return a line mapping (or the pipeline has to count offsets after the transform), or you'll trade a slow `explain` for a silently wrong one.**

Also: `SanitizePortableTranscript` returns the **unmodified input** when it can't parse or when everything was dropped (`transcript.go:403`). Fine as a lossless-fallback today; a trap if you make it the mandatory pre-redaction gate, since callers can't assume the output is sanitized.

## On the plan

Steps 1–3 are right and I'd do them as one change. Step 5's test is cheap. **Step 4 I'd defer** — it's the largest piece and sanitize-first already collapses 27MB → 77KB for Codex, so there'd be nothing left to be incremental about. Incremental redaction only pays off for agents whose transcripts are large in *readable* text (Claude Code with big tool outputs). Line-wise redaction is genuinely local so it's feasible, but compaction is not: `FullWithBoundary` merges streaming messages across lines, which is exactly why the boundary marker "rounds toward inclusion." Measure after 1–3, then decide.

Want me to implement 1–3 plus the offset fix, or write it up as a plan first?

content.text:
Traced it. Short answer: **yes, it's read — but not by the path you'd expect, and one of the three copies is write-only dead weight.**

## There are three copies of every transcript

| # | Location | Written | Read by anything? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Agent's own rollout (`~/.codex/sessions/…`) | by the agent | ✅ authoritative — condensation prefers this |
| 2 | `.entire/metadata/<session>/full.jsonl` on disk | raw, every Stop (`lifecycle.go:744`) | ❌ **no production reader** |
| 3 | Shadow-branch blob | redacted copy of #2 | ✅ four readers |

**Copy #2 is write-only.** Nothing reads it back. It exists solely as staging input for the shadow-tree walk — so every Stop writes 27MB to disk, reads it back, redacts it, and blobs it. The only disk read of that directory is `legacyFallbackTranscriptPath` (`rewind.go:625`), and that's the *legacy* `full.log` name, not `full.jsonl`.

## The shadow copy's four readers

| Reader | What it actually needs |
|---|---|
| `sessionHasNewContent` — `manual_commit_hooks.go:1643` | only `tree.Size()`. Never reads content. |
| `extractSessionData` — `manual_commit_condensation.go:1020` | **fallback only.** Comment: "prefer the live file … the shadow branch copy may be stale" |
| `explain <temp-sha>` — `explain.go:1608,1646,1655` | historical snapshot, and diffs against the *parent* shadow commit to compute checkpoint scope |
| `rewind` to an uncommitted checkpoint — `rewind.go:713` | historical snapshot, written back over the agent's live session file so the agent's memory matches the rewound code |

So for the main pipeline — condensation → `v1` → push — the shadow transcript is a **fallback, not the source**. Its genuinely load-bearing uses are a size probe, `explain` on a temp checkpoint, and rewinding the agent's memory.

## Could it be an offset instead of a snapshot?

That's the tempting simplification: the rollout is append-only, so checkpoint N's transcript is `prefix(live, offset_N)`. Store the offset, drop the blob. Four things break it:

1. **Rewind rewrites the live file** to a past state (`restoreSessionTranscriptFromShadow` → `agent.WriteSession`). The consumer of offsets is the same operation that invalidates them.
2. **Agent-side compaction isn't an append** — Codex emits `compacted` lines and Claude Code rewrites with a summary.
3. **Resume/fork** can start a fresh rollout file.
4. **Durability.** Agents rotate and GC old rollouts; users delete session dirs. Until condensation, the shadow copy is Entire's *only* record of uncommitted work.

(4) is the real justification. I'd keep the snapshot.

## What I'd actually change

The transcript is in the shadow branch **by accident, not by design.** `addDirectoryToChanges` (`ephemeral.go:990`) walks the whole metadata dir and redacts each blob generically — which is precisely *why* it's never sanitized and why redaction runs on raw ciphertext. The bug you started with is a symptom of the incidental walk.

So, without touching the shadow-branch concept:

- **Make the transcript an explicit tree entry**, written through the same prepare-for-storage pipeline as the committed path (sanitize → externalize → redact). Fixes the 47s and shrinks the blob ~99.7%.
- **Delete copy #2.** Redact in memory and blob directly; drop a 27MB write + 27MB read per Stop.
- The `tree.Size()` growth check keeps working, but `state.CheckpointTranscriptSize` then needs to be recorded in post-sanitize coordinates — same coordinate-consistency trap as the `CheckpointTranscriptStart` line drift I flagged earlier. Both come from mixing raw and stored coordinates.

**On killing the shadow branch outright:** the *file* snapshots are the product — that's rewind for uncommitted work, and git objects give you content-addressing, dedup, and crash-safety for free. I wouldn't remove it. What deserves removal is the incidental metadata-dir walk and the raw staging file, not the branch.

Want me to map what a deliberate shadow-tree write would look like, or keep pulling on whether `explain`'s parent-diff scoping could just use recorded offsets (it's the one reader that doesn't need the snapshot for durability reasons)?

the issue is: if we do the same sanitize+redact+extract stuff, then rewind will also modify your local session, now we also have "resume" but that's more a best effort thing, like we have to do necessary things since we move the transcript through a remote git repo and have no proper local copy at all mosty. But maybe then sanitize+extract+redact makes sense as a safety guard (if the agent local transcript is really gone on an old branch) but otherwise use the offset to modiy the actual file?

Your instinct is right, and there's a sharper version of the argument: **Thomi's step 2 would actively break rewind for Codex.**

Let me confirm what rewind writes back today and what metadata exists to hang an offset on.

content.text:
Yes — and there's a sharper version of your argument sitting in the function's own name.

## The sanitizer was built for the portable case only

```go
// SanitizePortableTranscript strips encrypted history fragments that cannot be
// replayed when Entire reconstructs a Codex rollout outside its original
// session context.
```
`codex/transcript.go:385`

"Outside its original session context" is the entire premise. A local rewind is *inside* the original session context — same machine, same rollout, same session. Running the portable transform there is a category error: you're paying a lossy conversion designed for a constraint that doesn't apply.

Which means **Thomi's step 2 — "use that transformation in every checkpoint path" — would regress rewind for Codex.** Today rewind restores a redacted-but-unsanitized transcript, so `encrypted_content` survives. Apply sanitization everywhere and rewind starts writing back rollouts with the reasoning payloads stripped. Worth confirming against a live Codex resume rather than taking the comment's word for it, but the direction is clear enough that step 2 shouldn't ship as written.

## Rewind already degrades the live session today

`restoreSessionTranscriptFromShadow` (`rewind.go:713`) writes the shadow blob back via `agent.WriteSession` — and that blob has been through the 8 redaction layers (`ephemeral.go:990` → `createRedactedBlobFromFile`). So **rewinding today replaces the user's live rollout with a secret-redacted copy.** Offset-based truncation fixes a current bug, not just a hypothetical one.

## Resume already got this right

`checkpoint_resume.go:50`: *"Existing local session logs are never overwritten unless `--force` is given."*

Resume prefers the untouched local file and treats the checkpoint copy as fallback. Rewind is the inconsistent one. Your proposal is really "make rewind behave like resume" — which is a consistency fix, not a new concept to justify.

## What the offset needs to be safe

A bare line number isn't enough, because the append-only assumption fails in exactly the cases that matter: agent-side compaction, session fork, and *a prior rewind*. Record **offset + a hash of the prefix**, then:

1. Hash the live file's first N lines. Match → truncate in place. Exact original bytes, zero loss.
2. Mismatch or file gone → restore from the stored sanitized copy, **and tell the user it's the lossy path**. That's a UX requirement; silently handing Codex a de-reasoned rollout is worse than saying so.

The prefix hash turns "is this still a prefix?" from an assumption into a check — which is the thing that makes the fallback tier honest.

## Where to put it

Not a tree entry. Shadow trees deliberately have **no `metadata.json`** — `ReadAgentTypeFromTree` sniffs agent config markers precisely because *"shadow branches don't have metadata.json"* (`common.go:932`). Don't invent one.

Use the **shadow commit trailer**. `trailers.FormatShadowCommit(msg, metadataDir, sessionID)` (`ephemeral.go:101`) already carries structured fields, and `ListCheckpoints` already parses trailers (`ephemeral.go:558-566`). Offset + prefix hash go there: no blob, no tree walk, no format migration.

Bonus: `explain <temp-sha>` currently computes checkpoint scope by reading the parent shadow commit's *entire* transcript and diffing (`explain.go:1646-1660`). With offsets in the trailer that collapses to arithmetic — two full transcript reads become zero.

## The resulting tiers

| Path | Source | Fidelity |
|---|---|---|
| Rewind, live file intact (normal case) | truncate agent's own rollout at recorded offset | **lossless** |
| Rewind, prefix check fails / file gone | stored shadow copy | lossy, announced |
| Resume same machine | existing local log (already the default) | lossless |
| Resume cross-machine / old branch | `v1` from remote | lossy by necessity — payload is unreplayable there anyway |

Note this is **complementary to, not a replacement for, the sanitize-first fix.** The stored copy still needs sanitize→externalize→redact ordering to get the 47s → 175ms win and the 99.7% size cut. What changes is that the stored copy stops being the *primary* restore source and becomes the safety net you described — which is also what finally makes it safe to sanitize it aggressively, since nothing on the happy path depends on its fidelity anymore.

One race worth noting: truncating a file the agent may be appending to. `WriteSession` has the same exposure today, so it's not new, but in-place truncation makes it slightly more likely to matter.

Traced every consumer. **No — dropping rewind doesn't free the shadow branch. But it does let you collapse it from a branch into a single ref, which is where the real cost is.**

## Who actually consumes the shadow tree

| Consumer | Needs | Survives dropping rewind? |
|---|---|---|
| **Attribution** — `manual_commit_attribution.go:215,260` | line-level content diffs `base→shadow→head` via `getFileContent(shadowTree, …)` | ✅ **and it's the real justification** |
| **Per-prompt attribution** — `manual_commit_hooks.go:2449` | shadow tip vs worktree at prompt start | ✅ |
| **Reverted-file detection** — `content_overlap.go:56,194` | shadow content vs staged/committed content | ✅ |
| **Transcript durability** — `extractSessionData` fallback | transcript blob when the agent's rollout is gone | ✅ |
| **Growth check** — `manual_commit_hooks.go:1643` | `tree.Size()` of the transcript blob | ✅ |
| `explain <temp-sha>` | transcript + parent-diff for scope | ⚠️ partial — see below |
| **Rewind** | historical file snapshots, restored to disk | ❌ gone |

Attribution is the one that matters. It does a three-way line diff — `base → shadow → head` — and the shadow tree is the **only** record of what the agent's work looked like before a human touched it. Without it, `base→head` can't separate agent lines from human lines, `shadow→head` post-checkpoint user edits vanish, and the agent-% number is simply unavailable. That's a shipped feature that lands in checkpoint metadata and gets pushed.

So rewind was never the load-bearing consumer. It was the only one that *wrote back*.

## The actual simplification hiding here

Every surviving consumer reads **only the tip**:

- `calculateSessionAttributions` resolves `shadowRef.Hash()` — the ref tip.
- `PromptAttribution` diffs the tip against the worktree at prompt start, then stores the *line counts* in session-state JSON (`accumulatePromptEdits`) — never a tree.
- `content_overlap` resolves the ref, takes the tip.
- `extractSessionData` and the size probe take the tip.

**Nothing walks shadow history except rewind and `explain <temp-sha>`.** So once rewind goes, the commit chain is write-only garbage — you're paying object retention for history no code reads.

That means: **shadow branch → single mutable snapshot ref.** One commit, replaced each Stop.

Be honest about what that does and doesn't buy: each Stop still builds a tree of the current snapshot, so per-Stop work is roughly unchanged. The win is **retained objects and repo growth** — today every session leaves an unread commit chain behind until cleanup. The per-Stop latency win comes from the transcript fixes we already discussed (sanitize-first, drop the write-only staging copy), not from this.

## Two things you'd have to decide deliberately

**1. Recovering uncommitted agent work goes away permanently.** Right now the chain is the only mechanism that can put deleted-then-regretted agent work back. Rewind being deprecated with "no replacement" already implies accepting that, but collapsing the chain makes it irreversible — you can't reintroduce the feature later without the history you stopped keeping. Worth being explicit that this is the call being made, not a side effect of cleanup.

**2. `entire checkpoint list` / `explain <temp-sha>` need metadata, not blobs.** These are the read-only "here are this session's pending checkpoints" views, and they're user-visible independent of rewind. But look at what they actually render: timestamp, session ID, prompt, transcript scope. Zero file content. So they don't need the snapshot chain — they need a cheap per-checkpoint metadata record. Which is exactly the trailer we discussed for the transcript offset: put offset + prefix hash + timestamp there and `explain`'s parent-diff (`explain.go:1646-1660`, two full transcript reads) becomes arithmetic against the live file.

## Net shape

```
snapshot ref (single commit, replaced each Stop)
├── working-tree files at tip     → attribution, overlap detection
└── transcript (sanitized)        → durability safety net only

append-only per-checkpoint metadata (trailers or a small log)
└── timestamp, session, prompt, transcript offset + prefix hash
    → checkpoint list, explain scope
```

The transcript work from earlier still lands unchanged — it's now purely a safety net, which is precisely what makes it safe to sanitize aggressively.

The thing I'd verify before committing to this: whether anything outside the CLI reads the shadow chain — the BFF or web UI showing pending/uncommitted checkpoints. I only traced this repo. Want me to check `entire.io` and the backend for shadow-ref consumers?
ok, so given that rewind is overwriting today and is deprecated, let's do this in steps, first the fix that applies the sanitation in the shadow branches, and next we can then move to refs

Let me look at the coordinate coupling before I touch anything — the growth check compares a session-state size against the shadow blob size, and shrinking that blob could silently break condensation.

**Transcript sanitization (before redaction).** Entire never modifies the agent's
own transcript, but the copy it stores goes through the agent's optional
`agent.TranscriptSanitizer` first, at the point Entire takes custody (the Stop path
in `lifecycle.go`, before `.entire/metadata/<session>/full.jsonl` is written). Codex
implements it to strip encrypted reasoning payloads and compaction blobs, which are
bound to the originating session and cannot be replayed out of a checkpoint.

Ordering matters in both directions: sanitizing first keeps non-replayable payloads
out of storage, and it spares the redaction layers from scanning ciphertext they
would only discard afterwards — base64 is the pathological input for the entropy
layer, so a large Codex rollout otherwise costs tens of seconds per Stop. The
transform is idempotent, so later write paths can call it without knowing whether an
upstream path already did.

is a growth baseline compared against the shadow transcript blob's size in
`sessionHasNewContent`, so it must be measured in the same (sanitized) coordinate —
see `CondenseResult.TranscriptSizeBaseline`. A raw baseline against a sanitized blob
makes the comparison false forever and the session silently stops condensing.

Step 1 is done and verified. Working tree only — nothing committed.

## What changed

**New generic capability** — `agent.TranscriptSanitizer` (`agent/agent.go`) + `agent.SanitizeTranscriptForStorage` (`agent/capabilities.go`). Resolved by type assertion with no `DeclaredCaps` gate, following `AsSidecarImageProvider`. Codex implements it (`codex/transcript.go`) by delegating to the existing `SanitizePortableTranscript`.

**Applied where Entire takes custody** — `lifecycle.go:744`, before `.entire/metadata/<session>/full.jsonl` is written. That file is the input the shadow-branch walk blobs and redacts, so sanitizing there fixes the shadow path at its source. The agent's own rollout is untouched.

**Consolidated the store's two hardcoded Codex checks** into one `sanitizeForAgentType` helper (`checkpoint/persistent.go`), covering the raw-transcript fallback path.

## Measured result

A 27.4 MB Codex rollout: **Stop hook 504 ms**, shadow blob **87 KB (0.32% of raw)**. Redaction alone on that content measured 47 s before. No timeout increase needed.

## Two things worth flagging

**A near-miss I caught mid-implementation.** I first had the store resolve the agent via `agent.GetByAgentType`, which read cleaner. It's unsafe: the registry is populated by package `init`, so the lookup only succeeds if something else in the binary imports `agent/codex`. Removing that import made sanitization silently degrade to a no-op — reintroducing the exact bug, with no signal. Reverted to explicit compile-time dispatch, with the reasoning in the comment so nobody "cleans it up" again.

That surfaced a second problem: **`mise run test:ci` reported exit 0 while `go test ./cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/` failed.** My own fault — I'd piped through `tail`, so I was reading `tail`'s exit code. Worth knowing that pattern hides failures; the re-run with `pipefail` gave a genuine `EXIT=0`.

**The coordinate coupling was real and load-bearing.** `SessionState.CheckpointTranscriptSize` is a growth baseline compared against the shadow blob's size in `sessionHasNewContent`. Shrinking the blob 99% while leaving the baseline raw makes `blobSize > baseline` false forever — sessions silently stop condensing after their first commit. Fixed via `CondenseResult.TranscriptSizeBaseline` (measured on the sanitized transcript), with a regression test. The codebase already had a comment warning about this exact trap from when image externalization hit it; I updated it.

## Verification

- New: 2 integration tests (RED→GREEN; sanitization + the growth guard) and 7 unit tests (idempotency, passthrough, nil-agent, fail-safe on nil return).
- `mise run fmt && mise run lint` → 0 issues. `mise run test:ci` → `EXIT=0`, vogon canary green.
- Docs updated: `docs/architecture/sessions-and-checkpoints.md` and `CLAUDE.md` — both called `full.jsonl` the "raw transcript", now inaccurate.

## Not in this step

**Post-commit condensation still redacts the raw transcript.** `manual_commit_condensation.go:319` runs `redactOrDrop` on the live rollout, so the 47 s cost remains on the commit path — the stored v1 transcript ends up sanitized, but only after redaction has already scanned everything. That's the original `persistent.go:1041`-vs-`1053` ordering bug, and it's a ~2-line fix in the pipeline I just touched (`sanitize → externalize → redact`). I left it out because you scoped step 1 to shadow branches, but it's the reason a commit can still stall — say the word and I'll fold it in before refs.

Also still open, unchanged by this step: the `CheckpointTranscriptStart` line-offset drift (counted on raw, applied to the sanitized stored transcript). Pre-existing, needs migration thought for in-flight sessions, and it's the thing the trailer + prefix-hash work would resolve properly.

fix(checkpoint): sanitize agent transcripts before redacting them

Entire's stored copy of a Codex rollout went into the shadow branch raw:
lifecycle wrote the untouched rollout to .entire/metadata/<session>/full.jsonl
and the generic metadata-dir walker redacted every blob without ever calling
SanitizePortableTranscript. So encrypted reasoning payloads and compaction
blobs landed in the shadow tree, and the eight redaction layers had to scan all
of that ciphertext first — base64 is the pathological input for the entropy
layer, which made a large rollout cost tens of seconds on every Stop.

Introduce agent.TranscriptSanitizer, an optional capability for agents whose
native transcript format carries state that cannot be replayed out of a
checkpoint, and apply it at the point Entire takes custody of a copy (the Stop
path, before full.jsonl is written). Codex implements it via the existing
SanitizePortableTranscript. The agent's own rollout is never modified.

A 27.4 MB rollout now checkpoints in ~500ms and stores 87 KB (0.32% of raw);
redaction alone on that content measured 47s before.

Also fix the coordinate coupling this introduces.
SessionState.CheckpointTranscriptSize is a growth baseline compared against the
shadow transcript blob's size in sessionHasNewContent, so shrinking the blob
while leaving the baseline on the raw transcript makes `blobSize > baseline`
false forever and the session silently stops condensing after its first commit.
CondenseResult.TranscriptSizeBaseline carries the sanitized size so both sides
stay in the same coordinate.

The checkpoint store dispatches on agent type explicitly rather than resolving
an agent via the registry: registry entries are populated by package init, so a
lookup only succeeds when something else in the binary happens to import
agent/codex, and when it doesn't sanitization silently degrades to a no-op —
reintroducing this exact bug with no signal.

Waiting on the CI re-run to confirm green before committing. Let me summarize where things stand.

**Commit 1** (`b8c726361`) — shadow-branch sanitization, already committed and verified.

**Commit 2** (staged in working tree) — the ordering fix, which turned out to be **two** call sites, not one:

| Path | Fix |
|---|---|
| Post-commit condensation | `prepareTranscriptForStorage` — extracted helper doing sanitize → externalize |
| Stop finalize (full-session rewrite) | `manual_commit_hooks.go:2846` — sanitize before `extractSessionImages` |

I only found the second because my test still failed after fixing the first: `finalizeAllTurnCheckpoints` independently rebuilds the stored transcript, so fixing condensation alone left the bug live.

**The ordering bug had a correctness consequence, not just a perf one.** Image externalization ran on the raw transcript, so an image embedded in a Codex `compaction` item got extracted into an asset blob + manifest entry — then sanitization dropped the transcript line referencing it. The result: an orphaned asset stored and pushed forever. That's what my RED test pins (2 assets → 1), and it's deterministic, unlike a timing assertion.

**Measured on a 27.4 MB rollout:** Stop 456 ms, commit/condense 506 ms. Both paths were previously paying the ~47 s redaction scan.

Two things worth flagging:

- **`maintidx` lint caught my first attempt** — inlining the rationale pushed `CondenseSession` past the complexity threshold. Extracting `prepareTranscriptForStorage` was the better shape anyway; the ordering contract now documents the pipeline rather than one call site.
- **CI failed once with a subprocess segfault** in `TestSessionIDConflict_ManuallyCreatedOrphanedBranch` (`transcript_path: ""` — no transcript involved). I verified it's the known pre-existing flake: passes 3× with my changes and 5× on the commit-1 tree. Re-running the full suite now rather than asserting green off a known-flaky run.

Docs updated in both commits (`sessions-and-checkpoints.md`, `CLAUDE.md`); the pipeline table now names all three paths so the next person doesn't miss the finalize one the way I initially did.

I'll commit once the suite comes back clean, and report the final state.

Done. Both commits are on `soph/sanitize-transcript-before-redact`, tree clean, Entire trailers attached automatically.

## The two commits

**`b8c726361`** — shadow-branch sanitization. New `agent.TranscriptSanitizer` capability, applied at the Stop path where Entire takes custody of its copy. Codex implements it. Plus the mandatory `CheckpointTranscriptSize` coordinate fix.

**`24589d46f`** — the ordering fix. Sanitize now runs *first* in condensation and in Stop finalize, giving `sanitize → externalize → redact` everywhere.

## What the ordering fix turned out to be

Not just perf. **Image externalization was running on the raw transcript**, and it walks every string leaf — so an image inside a Codex `compaction` item got lifted into an asset blob + manifest entry, and then sanitization dropped the transcript line referencing it. An orphaned asset, stored and pushed for the life of the checkpoint. The test pins it deterministically (2 assets → 1) rather than relying on a timing assertion.

**And it was two call sites, not one.** `finalizeAllTurnCheckpoints` rebuilds the stored transcript independently of `CondenseSession`. I only caught it because the test still failed after fixing condensation — worth knowing that path exists if you touch this again. The docs table now names all three paths for that reason.

## Measured

27.4 MB Codex rollout: **Stop 456 ms, commit/condense 506 ms**, stored blob 87 KB (0.32% of raw). Redaction alone on that content measured 47 s, so both hooks were previously well past any reasonable timeout — commit 1 alone would have left the commit path still stalling.

## Two process notes

- **`mise run test:ci | tail` silently swallows failures** — the pipeline exit code is `tail`'s. It reported success over a genuinely failing checkpoint package early on. Worth avoiding that pattern.
- **One CI run failed on a subprocess segfault** in `TestSessionIDConflict_ManuallyCreatedOrphanedBranch` (`transcript_path: ""`, no transcript involved). Verified pre-existing: 3× green with my changes, 5× green on the commit-1 tree. Final run: `EXIT=0`, zero FAIL lines, canary green.

## Still open, deliberately

- **`CheckpointTranscriptStart` line-offset drift** — counted on the raw transcript, applied to the sanitized stored one. Pre-existing; needs a migration story for in-flight sessions. The trailer + prefix-hash work resolves it properly.
- **Refs (step 2)** — collapsing the shadow branch to a single snapshot ref, since nothing but rewind and `explain <temp-sha>` reads past the tip.

Cleanup is done and verified, left uncommitted so you can review it against the two commits.

## Fixed (9)

**Reuse**
- `AsTranscriptSanitizer` hand-rolled the nil-check + type assertion that `builtinCapability[T]` already provides — the generic is documented for exactly this ungated case with three existing users. Now a one-liner.
- Added `TranscriptSanitizer` to the `DeclaredCaps` doc's exclusion list, which was already stale.
- Deleted `sanitizeRestoredTranscript` — a one-line pass-through that my new method turned into a *third* name for one transform. Callers retargeted.
- Added the missing `_ agent.TranscriptSanitizer = (*CodexAgent)(nil)` compile-time assertion, per that file's own convention.
- Replaced the duplicated hook-driver closure in `codex_image_externalize_test.go` with the extracted `codexHooker`/`applyPatchHook`, so the Codex hook stdin contract lives in one place.

**Efficiency**
- **Added a fast path to `SanitizePortableTranscript`** — a marker pre-scan plus a `changed` flag, so an already-sanitized transcript returns its original backing array instead of paying a deep JSON parse and two full-size copies. Measured: first pass 167 ms, redundant pass **628 µs**. This is what makes "every storage path calls it" actually affordable. Pinned by two new tests.
- `prepareTranscriptForStorage` now returns `sanitizedSize int64` instead of the multi-MB sanitized slice, which was being retained across redaction, chunking, and blob writes purely to read its length.

**Simplification**
- **Deleted `CondenseResult.Transcript`** — my change removed its last two readers, leaving a multi-MB field with zero consumers and a comment claiming a "trail titles" consumer that doesn't exist. Build confirmed it was dead.
- Trimmed the ordering rationale from five code copies to one canonical home (the interface doc) plus one-liners, and cut the `sanitizeForAgentType` comment from 15 lines to 5.

## Skipped (5)

- **Move the store's sanitize into the `TranscriptPath` fallback** (efficiency) — would have silently dropped real coverage. I checked: `agentimport` feeds the store **raw third-party rollouts** that bypass all three sanitizing paths. Two agents disagreed here; the one arguing for coverage was right. Kept the call and made it cheap instead, and rewrote the comment to name `entire import` as the actual reason it exists.
- **Thread the sanitized transcript through `HandleTurnEnd`** to stop finalize re-reading the live rollout — a genuine full-size redundant pass, but it needs a signature change across the turn-end chain. Deferred.
- **Read-side chokepoint** (`agent.ReadTranscriptForStorage` + `readLiveTranscript`) — architecturally the right answer, and it would fix the `CheckpointTranscriptStart` line drift for free by counting lines post-sanitize. Four read sites plus an untouched `ephemeral.go` task path; too wide for a cleanup pass.
- **`WriteOptions.Sanitize` func / "RedactedBytes implies sanitized"** — the deeper altitude fix that makes the store agent-agnostic. Real, but an API change touching `attach` and `agentimport`.
- **Compare blob hashes instead of sizes** for growth detection — would change intended behavior of `sessionHasNewContent`.

One correction to something I said earlier: I described the store's redundant sanitize passes as costing a full pass over the transcript. They run on *already-sanitized* bytes (41 KB, not 27 MB), so they were never as expensive as that implied. The finalize path's re-read is the one genuinely full-size redundant pass, and it's the item I deferred.

## Problem

Entire stores its own copy of an agent transcript in the shadow branch (every Stop) and in `entire/checkpoints/v1` (every commit). Codex rollouts carry state that cannot be replayed out of a checkpoint — encrypted reasoning payloads and compaction blobs, bound to the originating session. `codex.SanitizePortableTranscript` strips them, but it ran **last**, and on one path not at all:

- The Stop path wrote the **raw** rollout to `.entire/metadata/<session>/full.jsonl`, and the generic metadata-dir walker redacted every blob without ever sanitizing.
- Condensation and the Stop finalize rewrite externalized images and redacted the **raw** transcript; the checkpoint store sanitized only afterwards, on the way into the tree.

Two consequences:

**Performance.** Base64 ciphertext is the pathological input for redaction's entropy layer (`secretPattern` + Shannon ≥ 4.5). The 8 layers scanned megabytes of ciphertext that sanitization then discarded. Measured on a synthetic 27.4 MB Codex rollout: **redaction alone took 47 s**, at 0.26 MB/s. That is the timeout, and raising the timeout only hides it.

**Correctness.** Image externalization walks every string leaf, so an image embedded in a Codex `compaction` item was lifted into an asset blob + manifest entry — and then sanitization dropped the transcript line referencing it. The result was an **orphaned asset**, stored and pushed for the life of the checkpoint.

## Change

Every path that builds a stored transcript now runs the same pipeline in the same order: **sanitize → externalize images → redact**.

Sanitization is a new optional agent capability, `agent.TranscriptSanitizer`, applied via `agent.SanitizeTranscriptForStorage`. Codex implements it; the agent's own rollout is never modified. It is applied at:

| Path | Where |
|---|---|
| Stop / shadow branch | `lifecycle.go`, before `full.jsonl` is written |
| Post-commit condensation | `prepareTranscriptForStorage` in `manual_commit_condensation.go` |
| Stop finalize (full-session rewrite) | `manual_commit_hooks.go` |
| Safety net for callers with no live agent | `checkpoint.sanitizeForAgentType` |

## Results

Same 27.4 MB rollout, end to end through the real Codex hooks:

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Stop hook | (47 s in redaction alone) | **456 ms** |
| Commit / condense | (same scan again) | **506 ms** |
| Stored shadow blob | 27.4 MB | **87 KB** (0.32%) |

## Things reviewers should know

**The growth baseline had to move with it.** `SessionState.CheckpointTranscriptSize` is compared against the shadow transcript blob's size in `sessionHasNewContent`. Shrinking the blob ~99% while leaving the baseline measured on the raw transcript makes `blobSize > baseline` false *forever* — the session silently stops condensing after its first commit. `CondenseResult.TranscriptSizeBaseline` keeps both sides in the sanitized coordinate. There is a regression test for exactly this. The codebase already carried a warning about this trap from when image externalization hit it.

**The store dispatches on agent type explicitly, on purpose.** An earlier iteration resolved the agent via `agent.GetByAgentType`, which reads cleaner. It is unsafe here: the registry is populated by package `init`, so the lookup only succeeds when something else in the binary happens to import `agent/codex`. When it doesn't, sanitization silently degrades to a no-op — reintroducing this exact bug with no signal. The comment says so, so nobody "cleans it up" again.

**Sanitization has a fast path.** A marker pre-scan plus a change flag means an already-sanitized transcript returns its original backing array instead of paying a deep JSON parse and two full-size copies (167 ms → 628 µs). That is what makes calling it from every storage path affordable.

## Tests

- `TestCodexShadowBranch_SanitizesTranscript` — the shadow blob has no `encrypted_content` / compaction items, and still has the conversation.
- `TestCodexShadowBranch_GrowthStillDetectedAfterCommit` — a second commit still condenses a new checkpoint (the coordinate-coupling guard).
- `TestCodexCondense_NoAssetsFromSanitizedAwayContent` — an image in a `compaction` item is not externalized into an orphaned asset; the one in a real message still is.
- `TestSanitizePortableTranscript_{UnchangedInputReturnsSameBytes,IdempotentBytes}` — pins the fast path and byte-idempotency.
- 7 unit tests on the capability contract (idempotency, passthrough, nil agent, fail-safe on a nil return).

`mise run fmt && mise run lint` → 0 issues. `mise run test:ci` → pass, vogon canary green. Commit 1 verified to build and pass standalone, so the history bisects.

## Deliberately not in scope

- **Finalize re-reads the live rollout** and sanitizes it again — one genuinely full-size redundant pass per Stop. Fixing it means threading the sanitized bytes through the turn-end chain.
- **A read-side chokepoint** (`readLiveTranscript` / `ReadTranscriptForStorage`). The four raw reads are the real single point; doing it there would also fix the next item for free.
- **`CheckpointTranscriptStart` line-offset drift** — counted on the raw transcript, applied to the sanitized stored one. Pre-existing; needs a migration story for in-flight sessions.

content.text:
Verified. Here's the whole thing.

## Two coordinate systems for one number

`CheckpointTranscriptStart` is a **line number** meaning "this checkpoint's slice of the session starts here." The problem is that it's *counted* against one file and *applied* to a different one.

**Produced** on the raw live rollout — `countTranscriptItems` (`manual_commit_condensation.go:1170`) is just `len(strings.Split(content, "\n"))` over the transcript read straight from the agent:

```go
data.FullTranscriptLines = countTranscriptItems(state.AgentType, fullTranscript)  // raw
// → CondenseResult.TotalTranscriptLines → state.CheckpointTranscriptStart
```

**Consumed** against the stored, sanitized `full.jsonl` — `explain.go:1977` → `scopeTranscriptForCheckpoint` → `transcript.SliceFromLine`. Its own comment says so: *"CheckpointTranscriptStart indexes the stored format."*

And sanitization **deletes whole lines** for Codex — `compaction` and `compaction_summary` items return `nil, false` and vanish. So the stored file has *fewer* lines than the raw one, and the offset points too far in.

## Worked example

Turn 1 of a Codex session, condensed after line 5:

| Raw rollout (counted) | Stored `full.jsonl` (sliced) |
|---|---|
| 1 `session_meta` | 1 `session_meta` |
| 2 user "add feature" | 2 user "add feature" |
| 3 `reasoning` + `encrypted_content` | 3 `reasoning` (key stripped) |
| 4 `compaction` | — *dropped* |
| 5 assistant "done" | 4 assistant "done" |

`CheckpointTranscriptStart = 5`. But the stored file has only 4 lines.

`SliceFromLine(stored, 5)` walks newlines and hits `lineCount < startLine`, so it returns **nil** (`transcript/parse.go:133`). `entire explain --verbose` renders an empty "Transcript (checkpoint scope)" section. With more content after, you instead start N lines late and silently lose the first N lines of the turn — N being the number of compaction items before the offset.

## What's actually affected

Narrower than it sounds:

- **Affected:** `entire explain --verbose` scoping, and the compact-transcript boundary (`writeCompactTranscript` passes the same raw-coordinate `startLine` over post-sanitize bytes).
- **Not affected:** token accounting and growth detection. `CalculateTokenUsage(ctx, ag, data.Transcript, checkpointTranscriptStart, …)` and `currentPos <= state.CheckpointTranscriptStart` both compare against the **live** transcript — raw vs. raw, internally consistent.
- **Codex only.** It's the only agent with a line-dropping sanitizer, and only in sessions that actually contain compaction events.

## Why pre-existing, and why my change didn't touch it

The stored v1 transcript has been sanitized since before this PR (the old `if opts.Agent == AgentTypeCodex` at what was `persistent.go:1053`), and the offset has always been counted on raw. Both halves of the mismatch predate me.

If anything my change nudged one path toward *correct*: condensation's rare shadow-copy fallback now reads sanitized bytes, so a count taken there matches the stored file. Note the field's own doc comment still says *"Raw transcript (full.jsonl) line offset"* (`api/checkpoint/metadata.go:373`) — which is the confusion in miniature, since `full.jsonl` is the sanitized file.

## Why it needs a migration story

Because the number is persisted in two durable places, so you can't just switch the counting basis:

**1. Live session state** (`.git/entire-sessions/*.json`, `checkpoint_transcript_start`). It's a **watermark**: the next condensation scopes "from the previous watermark to now." Switch the basis mid-session and you compare a new sanitized-coordinate count against an old raw-coordinate watermark. Since sanitized < raw, the new count can be *lower* than the stored watermark — so `currentPos <= state.CheckpointTranscriptStart` concludes "no growth," or the delta covers the wrong window and a turn's content gets mis-scoped.

**2. Pushed checkpoint metadata** on `entire/checkpoints/v1` — already on remotes and other machines. Every historical checkpoint carries a raw-coordinate offset. A reader that assumes sanitized coordinates mis-slices all of them.

So a real fix needs one of:

- a basis marker (a version bump or a `transcript_offset_basis` field) so readers know how to interpret a given offset;
- write new offsets in stored coordinates and have readers branch on the new field's presence, accepting the old basis for old checkpoints;
- **the deeper fix** — sanitize at the *read* boundary (`readLiveTranscript` / `ReadTranscriptForStorage`), so Entire never holds raw bytes and there is only ever one coordinate system. Every count is then taken on already-sanitized data and the mismatch cannot arise. It still doesn't retroactively repair offsets already written, but it stops new drift and reduces the migration to "old checkpoints may mis-scope in `explain --verbose`."

That third option is why I flagged the read-side chokepoint as the natural next step — it fixes this as a side effect rather than needing its own mechanism.

Dug into it. Short answer: **it's about replayability, not privacy or size** — and the reason they're *dropped* rather than stripped is that there's nothing left once you strip them.

## What the two shapes are

Codex compaction produces two structurally different things, and the sanitizer treats them differently:

| Shape | Content | Treatment |
|---|---|---|
| `response_item` with `payload.type` = `compaction` / `compaction_summary` | `{"type":"compaction","encrypted_content":"…"}` — type tag + opaque blob, **nothing readable** | **dropped entirely** (`return nil, false`) |
| top-level `type: "compacted"` line with `payload.replacement_history` | real conversation — user/assistant messages that supersede earlier turns | **kept**, sanitized in place |

That asymmetry is the answer. A `compaction` item is a pure ciphertext carrier. Strip `encrypted_content` and you're left with `{"type":"compaction"}` — a semantically empty husk. Dropping it is the honest equivalent of stripping it.

Whereas a `compacted` line holds readable history, so `sanitizeCompactedLine` keeps the line and recurses: nested `reasoning` items just lose `encrypted_content`, nested `compaction`/`compaction_summary` items get dropped from the array by the same reasoning.

## Why sanitize at all

The function is `SanitizePortableTranscript`, introduced in a commit titled *"fixing codex resume"*, and the e2e test's payoff assertion is:

```go
require.NotContains(t, content, "invalid_encrypted_content")
```

So: these payloads are bound to the originating session — encrypted with state Entire doesn't hold. Hand them back to Codex when resuming from a checkpoint and the API rejects them. Stripping is what makes a checkpointed Codex transcript **replayable at all**. The size win (99.7%) is a side effect, not the motive.

## And this is where the drift comes from

Dropping is the **only** transform in the pipeline that changes line counts:

- stripping `encrypted_content` → rewrites a line, count unchanged
- `sanitizeHistoryItems` → removes array elements *inside* one line, count unchanged
- dropping a top-level `compaction` response_item → **count changes** ← the entire cause of the offset drift

Which suggests an alternative worth considering: **blank instead of drop.** Keep `{"type":"compaction"}` as a husk line. You trade a few bytes of meaningless marker for line-number stability — and the whole coordinate mismatch, plus its migration problem, evaporates. The risk is unknown Codex behavior on a `compaction` item with no payload, which is exactly what the e2e resume test exists to check. That's a cheaper fix than either the basis-marker or the read-boundary refactor, if it holds.

## One correction I owe you

Looking at the real fixtures, a `compaction` item contains *only* `encrypted_content` — no readable content, so no image data-URI can live there. My ordering test uses a synthetic shape (an image inside a compaction item) that real Codex probably never emits.

So the orphaned-asset consequence I put in the PR description as "a correctness bug, not just a slow one" is more accurately a **latent invariant violation**: the ordering was genuinely wrong, and my test does pin the property, but with real Codex data today nothing droppable contains an extractable image, so no orphaned asset would actually have been produced. The performance half of that PR's claim is real and measured; the correctness half is theoretical.

content.text:
Here's the answer, with the timeline pinned.

## The PR

**[#878 "Fixing codex resume"](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/878)** — merged 2026-04-10, commit `2e037d493` (2026-04-08), merge `372467035`. First shipped in **v0.5.4**.

## How long the line numbering has been broken

**Since 2026-04-10 — about four months.** And #878 is exactly where it broke, but not because it did anything wrong to the offsets. It never touched them.

The two halves were introduced independently, ten weeks apart:

| Date | Change | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **2026-01-31** | `faa4701f0` *"feat(explain): scope transcript and prompts to checkpoint boundaries"* | Started slicing the **stored** transcript by `CheckpointTranscriptStart`. Correct at the time — nothing altered the stored file, so raw line numbers *were* stored line numbers. |
| **2026-04-10** | **#878** added `transcript = codex.SanitizePortableTranscript(transcript)` to `checkpoint/committed.go` | Stored `full.jsonl` now has fewer lines than the raw rollout for Codex. The offset is still counted on raw. **Drift begins here.** |

I checked #878's diff against `manual_commit_condensation.go`: it did **not** touch `countTranscriptItems`, `FullTranscriptLines`, or the assignment to `CheckpointTranscriptStart`. It only *reused* `state.CheckpointTranscriptStart` to seed the compact transcript. So the mismatch arrived as a silent side effect of making the stored copy replayable — the January invariant ("stored line N == raw line N") was quietly invalidated by an April change in a different package, with nothing to catch it.

That's the classic shape of this bug class: an assumption held by one file, broken by another, with no assertion tying them together.

## Scope of the four months

Narrower than "broken for four months" sounds:

- **Codex sessions only** — the only agent with a line-dropping sanitizer.
- **Only sessions containing a top-level `compaction`/`compaction_summary` response item.** Nested ones inside `compacted.replacement_history` are removed from an array *within* one line, so they don't shift line counts.
- **Only two consumers**: `entire explain --verbose` checkpoint scoping, and the compact-transcript boundary. Token accounting and growth detection compare raw-against-raw and were never affected.
- Drift magnitude = number of dropped top-level compaction lines before the offset. Effect is either an empty "Transcript (checkpoint scope)" section or a slice starting N lines late.

So: a display-scoping bug in one command, for one agent, in compaction-bearing sessions, for four months — not silent data loss. The stored transcripts themselves are intact; only the *pointer into them* is off.

One thing worth noting given this history: the "blank instead of drop" option I mentioned would restore the January invariant rather than adding machinery to work around its absence. Keeping `{"type":"compaction"}` as a husk line makes stored and raw line counts equal again, and every offset already written — including the four months of existing checkpoints — becomes correct retroactively. That's a materially better outcome than a basis marker, if Codex tolerates the empty item on resume.

content.text:
Yes, we know — and there's something even simpler than counting drops. But that's not the blocker, and checking this corrected something I told you earlier.

## Computing it is the easy part

You don't even need a drop count. Since the offset is produced as "total lines at condensation," just count on the sanitized output:

```go
data.FullTranscriptLines = countTranscriptItems(agentType, sanitized)  // instead of raw
```

That yields a stored-basis offset directly. No mapping table, no per-line bookkeeping.

## The blocker is that one number serves two masters

`CheckpointTranscriptStart` has **five** consumers, split across both bases:

| Basis | Consumer |
|---|---|
| **raw** (live transcript) | `CalculateTokenUsage(ctx, ag, data.Transcript, offset, …)` — `data.Transcript` is the raw live file |
| **raw** | `currentPos <= state.CheckpointTranscriptStart`, where `currentPos` = `GetTranscriptPosition(livePath)` — `hooks.go:1898` |
| **raw** | `extractModifiedFilesFromLiveTranscript(ctx, state, offset)` — `hooks.go:1793, 1836` |
| **stored** (sanitized `full.jsonl`) | `explain --verbose` scoping via `scopeTranscriptForCheckpoint` |
| **stored** | compact-transcript boundary via `writeCompactTranscript(… startLine …)` |

So "just update the offset" **fixes the bottom two and breaks the top three.** Token accounting would slice the raw transcript by a sanitized index, and growth detection would compare a raw `currentPos` against a sanitized watermark — the same class of mismatch, moved rather than removed. That's why it isn't a one-line flip.

## Correcting my earlier answer

I said this "needs a migration story for in-flight sessions." That part is actually **tractable**, and your instinct is why: because sanitization is a pure function and the raw transcript is still on disk, a legacy raw watermark can be re-derived deterministically —

```
W_stored = countTranscriptItems(sanitize(rawPrefix(W_raw)))
```

— no version marker, no stored drop count, self-healing on the next condensation. (It assumes the rollout prefix is stable, i.e. compaction appends rather than truncates; worth confirming against Codex before relying on it.)

What I understated is the dual-basis consumer split above. *That's* the real obstacle, not the migration.

What stays unfixable by any offset arithmetic: **the four months of already-written checkpoint metadata.** Those offsets are raw-basis, and the raw transcript was never stored — so the drop count is unrecoverable from what's on the metadata branch.

## Ranked options

**1. Blank instead of drop** — keep `{"type":"compaction"}` as a husk line. Raw and stored line counts coincide again, so all five consumers agree, nothing to migrate, and **the existing four months of offsets become correct retroactively**. One-line sanitizer change, gated on whether Codex tolerates the empty item on resume (the e2e resume test is exactly the check). Strictly the best outcome if it holds.

**2. Sanitize at the read boundary** — Entire never holds raw bytes, so there is only one basis and the split cannot arise. Principled, and it also removes finalize's redundant re-read. Doesn't retroactively fix old checkpoints.

**3. Two explicit fields** — a raw offset and a stored offset, each consumer using the right one. Always works, but institutionalizes the dual basis and adds a field that future code will pick wrongly from.

I'd try #1 first precisely because it's the only one that repairs history rather than just stopping the bleeding — and it's the smallest change of the three. Want me to spike it and run the Codex resume e2e against it? That's the one test that would actually answer whether the husk is acceptable, and it needs a real API call, so I'd want your go-ahead before spending it.

content.text:
Mechanically yes — but checking it moved my ranking, because option 2 doesn't actually achieve what I claimed.

## The generic part does apply cleanly

A `readLiveTranscript` / `ReadTranscriptForStorage` helper is agent-agnostic, and `SanitizeTranscriptForStorage` is a **no-op for all 8 non-Codex agents** — none implements `TranscriptSanitizer`. So the refactor is behavior-preserving for Claude Code, Gemini, OpenCode, Cursor, Droid, Copilot CLI, Pi, and Vogon, and only changes Codex.

Worth saying explicitly: **there's no hidden drift for the other agents today.** Redaction, image externalization, and chunking all rewrite or split *within* line boundaries, so raw line/message counts equal stored ones everywhere except Codex.

## But it wouldn't give you one coordinate system

I described option 2 as "Entire never holds raw bytes, so there's only one basis." That's wrong, because a whole family of capabilities reads the raw file **by path**, straight off disk, bypassing any byte-level boundary:

| Capability | Called at |
|---|---|
| `GetTranscriptPosition(path)` — *this is raw-basis consumer #2* | `hooks.go:1888, 2719`, `state.go:123` |
| `ExtractModifiedFilesFromOffset(path, offset)` | `hooks.go:1969`, `lifecycle.go:820, 1136` |
| `ExtractPrompts(path, offset)` | `lifecycle.go:784`, `attach_transcript.go:68`, `rewind.go:855` |

To make those agree you'd have to either convert them to byte-based signatures or point them at a sanitized file. And they're implemented by **9 things — the 8 built-ins plus `external.Agent`**, which forwards them over the external-agent protocol (`external/external.go:300`, `external/capabilities.go:96`).

So converting the signatures is a **wire-format change for third-party agents.**

The "point them at a sanitized file" variant looks tempting because Entire already materializes one — `.entire/metadata/<session>/full.jsonl` has been sanitized since commit 1. But it's only refreshed at Stop, and `GetTranscriptPosition` is consulted *mid-turn*, so it'd be stale exactly when needed. Fixing that means rewriting a multi-MB file more often on a hot path — trading the problem for the one we just fixed.

## What that does to the ranking

Option 2's cost scales with agent count and reaches the external protocol, while its benefit here is Codex-only. That's a bad trade for a display-scoping bug in one agent, so I'd demote it as *the fix for this*.

**Option 1 (blank instead of drop) now looks clearly best**: it makes both bases coincide without touching a single agent interface, needs no migration, and retroactively corrects the four months of existing offsets. One line in the Codex sanitizer.

A read helper is still worth doing — just for different reasons: it de-duplicates the `resolveTranscriptPath` + `os.ReadFile` pair that's copied three times, and it's what kills finalize's redundant full-size re-read. Those are general wins. It just shouldn't be sold as the coordinate fix.

**Option 1 works.** Codex 0.143.0 accepts a compaction item with its payload stripped.

The logged evidence — `payload keys: [type]` — is the whole answer: the restored rollout contains `{"type":"response_item","payload":{"type":"compaction"}}`, the line survives, and `codex resume` reached the prompt with no `invalid_encrypted_content`.

## Why the first green run didn't count

The first run passed, but I couldn't prove it exercised the change — the e2e fixture only had *nested* compaction items, and nesting is unaffected by this change. So I added a top-level one plus a hard coverage assertion, and the second run **failed**. That failure was my helper's fault, not the fix's, but it surfaced something real:

**`entire resume` doesn't overwrite the agent's rollout — it writes a new one.** Same session id, new timestamped filename, so the home ends up with both:

```
original: rollout-2026-08-05T13-29-32-019fd1af-…jsonl   (local time, still has encrypted_content)
restored: rollout-2026-08-05T11-29-32-019fd1af-…jsonl   (UTC, stripped)
```

`findCodexRollout` asserts exactly one rollout, which is correct pre-resume and wrong after. Worth knowing independently of this work — and note the two filenames differ by timezone, which is its own latent oddity.

## What's now verified

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Restored rollout has a top-level compaction item | ✓ `payload keys: [type]` |
| Its encrypted payload is stripped | ✓ |
| No `encrypted_content` anywhere in the restored file | ✓ |
| The `compacted` line survives | ✓ |
| `codex resume` reaches the prompt | ✓ |
| No `invalid_encrypted_content` | ✓ |

Plus, locally: `mise run fmt && lint` → 0 issues, `test:ci` → `TEST_EXIT=0`.

## The change

`sanitizeRolloutLine` now treats `compaction`/`compaction_summary` exactly like `reasoning` — strip `encrypted_content`, keep the line — rather than dropping the line. Nested items inside `replacement_history` are still removed, since array removal can't shift line numbers.

Three existing tests had to be updated because they **codified the drift as expected behavior**. The most telling is `TestUpdateCommitted_CodexCompactSanitizedLikeInitialWrite`: given `[alpha, compaction, beta, gamma]` with `CheckpointTranscriptStart: 2`, it required **`beta` to be absent** from the checkpoint slice. That absent `beta` *was* the bug, asserted as correct. It now yields `[beta, gamma]`.

One honest limit: the sanitizer strips only the `encrypted_content` key, so a future Codex version stashing ciphertext under a different key would slip through — but that's pre-existing behavior for `reasoning` items, and I kept it uniform rather than blanking to a bare `type` (which would be more robust for stripping and riskier for replay). My own integration fixture had used an invented `payload.blob` key; I corrected it to the real shape.

input.content:
## Problem

`CheckpointTranscriptStart` marks where a checkpoint's slice of a session begins. It is **counted on the agent's raw rollout** but **applied to the stored, sanitized `full.jsonl`** — and for Codex those two files had different line counts, because `SanitizePortableTranscript` dropped `compaction` / `compaction_summary` lines outright.

So every offset into a stored Codex transcript was too large by the number of dropped lines before it. `transcript.SliceFromLine` then either starts N lines late or, when the offset exceeds the stored length, returns nothing.

```
raw rollout (counted)              stored full.jsonl (sliced)
1 session_meta                     1 session_meta
2 user "add feature"               2 user "add feature"
3 reasoning + encrypted_content    3 reasoning (key stripped)
4 compaction                       — dropped
5 assistant "done"                 4 assistant "done"

CheckpointTranscriptStart = 5, but the stored file has 4 lines.
```

**Broken since 2026-04-10** (#878, first shipped in v0.5.4) — roughly four months. #878 never touched the offsets; it added sanitization to the committed-write path and silently invalidated an invariant introduced ten weeks earlier in `faa4701f0` ("feat(explain): scope transcript and prompts to checkpoint boundaries"), which had been correct when nothing altered the stored copy.

Nothing caught it because the assumption lived in one package and was broken from another. In fact a test grew up around the symptom and asserted it as correct — see below.

### Scope

Narrower than it sounds, and no data was lost:

- **Codex only** — the only agent with a line-dropping sanitizer. Redaction, image externalization, and chunking all rewrite or split *within* line boundaries, so raw and stored counts match for every other agent.
- Only sessions containing a **top-level** `compaction`/`compaction_summary` item. Items nested in a `compacted` line's `replacement_history` are array elements — removing them cannot shift line numbers.
- Affects `entire explain --verbose` checkpoint scoping and the compact-transcript boundary. **Token accounting and growth detection are unaffected** — they apply the offset to the raw live transcript, so they were always internally consistent.

## Fix

Treat `compaction`/`compaction_summary` exactly like `reasoning`: strip `encrypted_content`, **keep the line**. Four lines of production change.

Nested items in `replacement_history` are still removed outright, since array removal can't shift line numbers.

Why this over the alternatives:

- **It repairs history.** Raw and stored line counts coincide again, so the offsets already written across four months of checkpoints become correct retroactively. Nothing else does that — the raw transcript was never stored, so a drop count can't be recovered after the fact.
- **No migration.** No basis-marker field, no version gate, no re-derivation of in-flight session watermarks.
- **No agent interface change.** The alternative of sanitizing at the read boundary would have to reach `GetTranscriptPosition` / `ExtractModifiedFilesFromOffset` / `ExtractPrompts` — path-based capabilities implemented by 8 built-in agents *and* forwarded over the external-agent protocol, so it would be a wire-format change for third-party agents.

## Verification

The open question was whether Codex tolerates a compaction item with no payload. Answered with a real `codex resume` against Codex CLI 0.143.0:

```
restored top-level compaction item, payload keys: [type]
```

The rollout `entire resume` writes now contains `{"type":"response_item","payload":{"type":"compaction"}}`, Codex loads it, reaches the prompt, and prints no `invalid_encrypted_content`.

Two things were needed to make that test mean anything:

1. **The e2e fixture only had *nested* compaction items**, which this change doesn't affect — so it would have passed without exercising the fix. It now also appends a top-level one.
2. **A coverage assertion** (`assertRestoredCompactionStripped`) that fails if the restored rollout lacks the payload-less compaction shape. Worth having permanently: it's the difference between "green" and "green *and* covered".

## Tests that had to change

Three existing tests pinned the old drop behavior. The notable one is `TestUpdateCommitted_CodexCompactSanitizedLikeInitialWrite`: given `[alpha, compaction, beta, gamma]` with `CheckpointTranscriptStart: 2`, it required **`beta` to be absent** from the checkpoint slice. That missing `beta` *was* the bug, asserted as expected behavior. It now correctly yields `[beta, gamma]`.

`mise run fmt && mise run lint` → 0 issues. `mise run test:ci` → pass, vogon canary green.

## Notes

- The sanitizer strips only the `encrypted_content` key, so ciphertext under a different key would survive. That is pre-existing behavior for `reasoning` items and is kept uniform here rather than blanking payloads to a bare `type` — more robust for stripping, riskier for replay.
- Incidental finding: `entire resume` does **not** overwrite the agent's rollout; it writes a fresh one for the same session id under a new timestamped name, so the Codex home holds both afterwards. The test helper had to account for that.

## Why #1901 needs a touch either way

Its `codex_shadow_sanitize_test.go` (which only exists on that branch) asserts the **old** behavior:

1. `!strings.Contains(stored, "compaction")` — expects the line dropped.
2. Its fixture puts ciphertext under an invented `payload.blob` key. Since the sanitizer only strips `encrypted_content`, that ciphertext would survive once PR B lands and the "ciphertext gone" assertion would fail.
3. Its ordering test relies on a top-level compaction line being *dropped* to orphan an asset — a scenario PR B removes.

So whichever merges second breaks the other. The fix is three edits to that one file, all defensible on their own merits: use the **real** `encrypted_content` key (the fixture was simply wrong — real Codex uses it), scope the assertion to intent (ciphertext and the key are gone) rather than to drop-vs-strip, and retarget the ordering test at the nested-history case, which is the one place sanitization still discards content.

After that, either PR can merge first. I already have all three edits written — they're in the stash from the earlier stacked attempt.

Once CI comes back I'll commit B, push, open the PR, then push the compatibility commit to #1901.

I'll hold here until the suite reports. To confirm the plan we've converged on:

**One PR (#1901), three commits** — each internally consistent so the history still bisects:

| Commit | Fix |
|---|---|
| `79ef6b8d3` | Shadow-branch sanitization + the `TranscriptSanitizer` capability + growth-baseline coordinate fix |
| `35f194faf` | Sanitize before externalize/redact (condensation + finalize) |
| *new* | Keep compaction lines so stored transcripts stay line-aligned |

This drops the compatibility fixup entirely — the `codex_shadow_sanitize_test.go` edits land in the third commit alongside the change that requires them, rather than needing to be back-ported to keep two PRs from breaking each other.

The one tradeoff worth naming: the PR now mixes a perf/ordering fix with a **behavioral** change to Codex replay (the payload-less compaction item, validated by the paid e2e). If that ever needs backing out because Codex tightens its deserializer, it's a single-commit revert rather than a single-PR revert — which is why I'm keeping it as its own commit rather than squashing it in.

The isolated CI run currently finishing is still useful either way: it validates the sanitizer change against plain `main`, independent of the other two commits, which is evidence I wouldn't get once it's stacked.

Then: commit, re-run the full suite on the stacked branch, update the PR title and description to cover all three fixes, and push.
